title: MFP Cash Bridge for Independent Pharmacies
one_liner: Reconciliation plus short-term financing for the cash gap independent pharmacies now carry between dispensing at Medicare's negotiated price and getting the manufacturer refund.
customer: Independent pharmacy owners (about 18,000 US stores) with heavy Medicare Part D volume, who are being asked to float thousands of dollars a week.
problem: The first ten Medicare-negotiated 'maximum fair prices' took effect January 1, 2026. Pharmacies buy at wholesale acquisition cost, dispense at the lower MFP and are refunded later through the Medicare Transaction Facilitator, with refunds due within 14 days but the clock starting only when manufacturers receive the data. An analysis for NCPA estimated weekly cash-flow shortfalls above $10K per pharmacy, and a member survey found over 90% of independents are considering not stocking or have stopped stocking one or more of the drugs.
solution: Step one is software: read pharmacy-management system exports and MTF remittance data, reconcile every MFP claim against refunds received, flag underpayments and late refunds, and forecast next week's cash gap. Step two is an advance product: fund verified pending MFP refunds at a small fee, repaid automatically when the MTF payment lands.
why_now: MFP has been live since January 2026, and cash-flow strain is documented. The second negotiation cycle, effective January 2027, adds 15 more drugs (including semaglutide products), so volume and float will grow sharply. Independent pharmacies are already squeezed by PBM reimbursement and store closures, and wholesalers and PBMs have little incentive to solve this.
revenue_model: $149-299 per pharmacy per month for reconciliation and alerts. 0.5-1.5% fee per advance, with a short 14-30 day duration. Warehouse-line financing spread as volume grows.
non_obvious_insight: This is receivables finance in disguise. Refunds owed by big manufacturers through a federal facilitator are among the best-quality, most verifiable small-business receivables in healthcare. The reconciliation software is the underwriting engine, so a small team can start with software, prove default rates are near zero, and then raise a cheap credit line. Being the trusted data layer also positions you for the 2027 and 2028 waves.
first_30_days: Partner with a state pharmacy association or NCPA-affiliated buying group. Recruit 10-15 pharmacies and ingest exports from PioneerRx, Rx30 or QS/1. Sell a $149/month MFP reconciliation dashboard that finds unpaid refunds. Run a free 'cash gap audit' to generate leads. After 60-90 days of clean data, approach a specialty lender for a small advance pilot.

title: Canary Errors: Measure If Human Reviewers Still Catch Mistakes
one_liner: Phishing-simulation for 'human in the loop': plant known, harmless defects in AI drafts headed to human reviewers and sell the measured catch-rate as audit-grade proof of oversight.
customer: Risk, compliance, and legal-ops heads at 20-500 lawyer firms, medical-coding/RCM companies, claims-review shops, and AML/KYC alert-review BPOs. The malpractice and E&O carriers and brokers that cover them are the second payer and the distribution channel.
problem: Every AI risk policy ends with 'a human reviews it.' Nobody measures whether that human still catches errors. Automation bias means that as the AI gets 98% right, reviewers drift into rubber-stamping. Clients, insurers and regulators now ask for evidence of effective oversight. Lawyers have been sanctioned in hundreds of cases for fabricated AI citations, and Deloitte Australia refunded part of a government fee in 2025 over AI-hallucinated errors in a report. Firms can show that a review step exists but cannot show that it works.
solution: A thin layer between the AI draft and the reviewer: a Word/DMS plugin or queue middleware. It seeds a small percentage of items with synthetic, known-answer defects: swapped case citations, transposed numbers, altered party names, wrong ICD or CPT codes. Nothing seeded ever ships, because a defect the reviewer misses is caught by the system before release, and the reviewer gets an instant 'gotcha' micro-lesson. It records catch, miss and time per reviewer and per workflow, adapts difficulty, and outputs an 'Oversight Effectiveness Report' mapped to EU AI Act human-oversight duties, ISO 42001, SR 11-7 and client outside-counsel guidelines. The end state is a vigilance score that insurers can price against.
why_now: Agentic workflows in 2025-26 push more volume through single-click 'approve' steps. Courts and clients now punish unreviewed AI output. EU AI Act human-oversight obligations for high-risk systems are coming, even with the timeline under revision. Insurers launching AI-specific coverage (Lloyd's-backed products, AI-underwriting startups) have no data on whether human controls actually work.
revenue_model: Per-reviewer seat at $30-90/month; workflow-level enterprise licenses at $20-100k/yr; insurer-branded 'verified oversight' certificates. Later, a data partnership with carriers that gives premium credits for high catch-rates.
non_obvious_insight: The market treats human review as a binary control ('there is a human'), but it is a decaying skill: the better the AI, the worse the human vigilance, as with airline autopilot. Whoever owns the catch-rate dataset becomes the credit bureau of human oversight, and insurers will price off it. It is also a wedge into every regulated workflow, because seeding defects needs no access to the underlying model.
first_30_days: Build a .docx defect injector for contract and brief review (citation swaps, number transpositions, defined-term drift). Recruit 3 small firms or legal-ops teams and one legal-malpractice broker as design partners. Run a free two-week baseline audit on about 10 lawyers and publish an anonymized benchmark ('the average associate catches X% of seeded citation errors') for PR and inbound. Convert to $2-5k paid pilots.

title: Fiduciary Collection Executor for Heirs
one_liner: A service that inventories, appraises and sells inherited card, comic, toy and coin collections for estate lawyers and executors, with an audit trail built for fiduciary liability.
customer: Probate and estate attorneys, trust officers, professional fiduciaries and family executors, billed per estate.
problem: Collections built by boomers and Gen X now carry five- to seven-figure values after record card prices, but heirs have no idea what they hold. 'We buy collections' buyers lowball, and executors are liable if they sell below fair value. Large estates and donations also need qualified appraisals.
solution: Photo-inventory intake (on-site or shipped kit), visual identification and comps, graded-versus-raw triage, sign-off by a qualified appraiser, and sale through the best channel (auction house, game store, streaming seller) under a published fee schedule. The output is an estate-ready valuation report with full custody and sale documentation.
why_now: Card prices are at records ($16.5M for a PSA 10 Pikachu Illustrator, $1.4M for a PSA 9). Visual AI has cut cataloging cost sharply. The wealth transfer is under way.
revenue_model: A flat inventory and appraisal fee ($500-3,000) plus a 10-15% sale commission. Referral relationships with law firms.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is not the collector but the fiduciary, who carries legal liability. Liability aversion unlocks budget, and the moat is trust artifacts (documented process, appraisal compliance) that any dealer cannot offer because the dealer sits on the other side of the trade.
first_30_days: Give a talk to 15 probate attorneys and 5 fiduciaries in one metro titled 'What is in Grandpa's basement.' Offer a $299 rapid triage, partner with a certified appraiser, and close the first 5 estates.

title: Turn Gray-Market Retatrutide Demand Into Trial Enrollment
one_liner: Intercept people searching to buy unapproved obesity drugs and route them, screened, to active trials that pay by the qualified referral.
customer: CROs, sponsors and trial sites running obesity and metabolic trials (paying per qualified lead or randomized patient), with the consumer as the traffic source.
problem: Sponsors struggle to recruit GLP-1-naive participants because prior GLP-1 use is an exclusion criterion and 22% of households already have a user. Meanwhile, non-trial retatrutide use grew ~1.8x per quarter, 71% of traced users bought outside trials, and Australia issued a liver and kidney injury alert in Jun 2026.
solution: A compliance-reviewed 'legitimate access' site and search and social funnel that meets intent ('retatrutide', 'triple agonist'), explains the risks, pre-screens (BMI, comorbidities, naive or washout status, geography) and refers to nearby enrolling Phase 2/3 sites. It screens out people who already took unapproved product where the protocol excludes them, and sponsors pay on qualified referral or randomization.
why_now: Retatrutide's Phase 3 program and Lilly's planned Q1 2027 filing are peak-hype. FDA and Lilly takedowns (>14,000 listings) push searchers toward risk. Pills at $149 are draining the classic trial pool, so recruitment cost per patient is rising.
revenue_model: Est. $150-500 per qualified referral and $2-6k per randomized patient, paid by CROs and sites, with performance tiers.
non_obvious_insight: Enforcement cannot remove demand. The highest-intent audience in obesity pharmacology is currently monetized by gray-market vendors, while trial sponsors pay per head for exactly the same people.
first_30_days: Build three landing pages and a screener reviewed by a regulatory consultant. Register with 3-5 enrolling sites and one CRO recruiter. Spend ~$3k on search and social ads for 'retatrutide clinical trial' style queries (check ad-policy limits) and deliver the first 50 pre-screened leads on a pay-per-qualified-referral contract.

title: Independent Robot Bake-Off and Acceptance Lab
one_liner: A neutral test cell where warehouse buyers watch robots handle their own SKUs and pallets before signing, with published, verified throughput numbers.
customer: Mid-size 3PLs, grocers and retailers (roughly 50-500k sq ft) evaluating palletizing, picking or humanoid pilots. Robot vendors are a second payer (for certification), and lenders and insurers are a third.
problem: Vendors control the demo. Buyers cannot verify throughput on their own product mix, and pilots eat 6-12 months. Funding is running far ahead of proof: Maven raised a $100M Series A with about 8 robots deployed, Agility booked $1.8M of revenue against a $2.5B SPAC valuation, and early 1X NEO demos were largely teleoperated.
solution: Rent a 20-30k sq ft cell in a logistics hub. Buyers ship 200 pallets or 500 SKUs. Vendors run their robots under a standard protocol. The lab logs picks per hour, error rate, human-intervention minutes, teleop minutes and mean time between failures, then issues a 'Verified Throughput' report. Buyers pay per bake-off, and vendors pay to list certified results and retest after software updates.
why_now: In 2026 procurement teams face a flood of unverifiable claims: about 22k humanoids shipped in H1, nine-figure rounds go to companies with a handful of deployed units, and buyers want outcome pricing. Nobody independent sits between vendors and buyers.
revenue_model: $15-40k per buyer-commissioned bake-off, $25-75k a year per vendor for certification and retests, and data licensing of failure-mode datasets to insurers and lenders.
non_obvious_insight: The industry's binding constraint is trust in claims, not capability. Vendors will pay for independent verification because their real bottleneck is a 9-12 month sales cycle (compare UL, J.D. Power, Wirecutter). The failure-mode data becomes an asset that insurers, lenders and model developers all want.
first_30_days: Rent demo floor space inside a friendly integrator's or 3PL's idle mezzanine. Sign 2 mid-size 3PLs to paid bake-offs of 3 vendors each, and give vendors a free first test in exchange for the right to publish. Release the public methodology and a first leaderboard of 'intervention minutes per hour'.

title: Permit-as-Firmware Groundwater Pump Governor
one_liner: A smart pump controller that hard-enforces a farmer's groundwater allocation and lets an agent trade unused acre-feet with neighbors before the pump ever exceeds its limit.
customer: Irrigated growers (almonds, pistachios, alfalfa, wine grapes) in California's regulated groundwater basins, especially San Joaquin Valley subbasins with adopted allocations and overpumping penalties. Groundwater sustainability agencies (GSAs) are the channel and co-payer.
problem: Allocations are enforced after the fact from meter reads. Kings County's agency, for example, set a $500-per-acre-foot charge for pumping above base allocation, with penalties slated after the 2026 water year. Probationary subbasins (Tule, Tulare Lake) add $300-per-well registration and a $20-per-acre-foot state fee. Farmers overshoot by accident, water trades run through brokers and phone calls, and GSAs cannot verify compliance without costly audits.
solution: A retrofit device on the well's starter or VFD, tied to a certified flow-meter reader, keeping a live allocation ledger. It soft-throttles as the budget nears zero, and can hard-stop with a paid override that 'borrows' at the penalty price. The grower's dashboard or agent can pre-bid to buy or sell units on a subbasin exchange. The GSA receives a read-only, tamper-evident compliance feed and can give fee discounts for participating wells.
why_now: Allocation-based enforcement begins in earnest with the 2027 water year, and the state has already put two San Joaquin Valley subbasins on probation. Water prices and fallowing pressure make trading valuable. Cellular and LoRa IoT and smart motor starters are now cheap.
revenue_model: $1.5-3k per well install, $50-150 per month per well, a 1-2% fee on water trades, and GSA grants or fee credits that subsidise compliance metering.
non_obvious_insight: The law is already a constraint. The product turns a legal budget into a physical budget, like a hard credit limit on a card. Growers want the stop because it converts unpredictable $500-per-acre-foot penalties into a controllable budget, and GSAs want it because self-reporting becomes verified data. Sell it as insurance against fines, not as smart irrigation.
first_30_days: Pick one subbasin with adopted allocations and penalties. Recruit 3 pump-service companies as install partners, since they own the relationship with the well. Pilot free on 5 wells in exchange for testimonials and data. Ask the GSA general manager for a compliance-metering pilot grant.

title: Executor-of-Last-Resort for Solo Agers
one_liner: A subscription that names a licensed fiduciary as your executor and runs daily wellness checks, so a childless retiree isn't found weeks late and handed to a court-appointed stranger.
customer: Unpartnered or childless adults 65+ with $100K-$1.5M estates (too small for most corporate trustees, too large to ignore), plus their elder-law attorneys, senior living communities and Area Agencies on Aging.
problem: Solo agers have no obvious executor, agent or emergency contact, and named friends or nieces often flake. Japan shows the downstream effect: 37,227 people living alone were found dead at home in H1 2024, nearly 4,000 undiscovered for over a month. The US has no equivalent service layer, and intestate estates go to public administrators.
solution: A 'Stewardship Plan'. (a) A licensed professional fiduciary or trust company partner agrees to serve as successor agent and executor. (b) Passive wellness signals (phone, smart speaker, utility use, optional wearable) plus a daily automated or human check-in escalate to neighbors and welfare checks. (c) A digital go-bag holds accounts, medications, pets, keys and funeral wishes. (d) At death it triggers funeral instructions, securing the house, clear-out and estate administration for a fee schedule.
why_now: Cheap ambient signals and voice-AI check-in calls make monitoring inexpensive. Death care is proving roll-up-able (Everstory, SCI), yet no one serves the years before death for people without heirs. Estates and consolidator data show volume is flat, so services attached to existing customers are where growth sits.
revenue_model: $39-$79/month subscription, executor fees at death (often statutory, a few percent of the estate), margin on clear-out and estate services, and B2B fees from senior living and AAAs.
non_obvious_insight: The first customer isn't dying. She is buying certainty that someone competent shows up on the worst day. Subscriptions fund the acquisition of a low-cost executor book that pays out later.
first_30_days: Partner with a licensed fiduciary in one state. Sign 3 elder-law attorneys. Recruit a 30-person waitlist through senior centers and 'elder orphan' groups. Charge $99 setup plus $49/month and run the daily check-in calls manually at first.

title: Capacity-Attested Wishes Recordings for Estate Attorneys
one_liner: Elder-law attorneys add a clinician-scored capacity note and a hash-sealed, attorney-controlled recording of the client's stated wishes to every will or trust signing, so heirs cannot wave the evidence away as a deepfake or as undue influence.
customer: Solo and small-firm elder-law and estate attorneys (they pay per client and mark it up), plus trust companies and bank wealth desks that handle contested-estate risk.
problem: A roughly $6T wealth transfer is under way, probate and estate cases rose about 32% from 2020 to 2024, and the heirs are Gen X and millennial executors. Cheap voice and video cloning means any real recording of 'what Dad said' can now be dismissed as fake, and undue-influence contests keep coming. Many attorneys avoid video because a shaky performance can backfire. Solo agers with no family have nobody to vouch for their wishes at all.
solution: A packaged signing workflow. (1) A 20-minute structured capacity assessment by a telehealth geriatric nurse practitioner or neuropsychologist, timed to the signing day. (2) A guided recording captured in an app that signs at capture with device attestation and a C2PA-style manifest, plus an independent RFC 3161 timestamp. The attorney decides what is retained. (3) An escrow vault that releases to the named executor on receipt of a death certificate. Output is a one-page verification link a probate judge can check without trusting the platform.
why_now: The oldest boomers turned 80 in 2026. FDA-cleared Alzheimer's blood tests (May and Oct 2025) will create a large biomarker-positive but still-competent population whose later wills will be attacked. C2PA 2.3 is mature and TikTok joined in Jul 2026. Voice cloning is good enough that courts and opposing counsel will start treating unsigned recordings as suspect.
revenue_model: $295-495 per client package billed to the law firm (clinician gets about $120, the rest is platform revenue), $99 a month per firm for vault storage and verification links, and later an enterprise tier for trust companies. Long-term escrow storage fees are recurring.
non_obvious_insight: The valuable evidence is not the video. It is a contemporaneous capacity finding made during the pre-dementia 'lucid window' that blood-test diagnosis is about to make very common. Provenance tech simply makes that finding, and the wishes on record, impossible to dismiss as synthetic. Attorneys buy this as malpractice and litigation insurance, not as a media product.
first_30_days: Sign 3 to 5 elder-law firms as design partners through state bar elder-law sections. Contract two geriatric NPs at a per-assessment fee. Build the capture app on off-the-shelf C2PA and timestamping libraries. Run 10 live signings at a discounted $195 and turn each into a case study for the next firm.

title: Blinded Self-Trials for Your Supplement Stack
one_liner: Mail-order double-blind crossover kits that tell you which of your own supplements move your own labs and wearable data, and which you can stop paying for.
customer: Adults 35-65 spending $60-300 per month on vitamins, longevity stacks and nootropics. About 8 in 10 Americans take supplements, per a Pew survey published in September 2026. First reached through biohacker communities and health podcasts; later through functional-medicine and longevity practitioners who want evidence for their patients.
problem: Nobody knows whether magnesium, ashwagandha, creatine, NMN or fish oil does anything for them. Population trials show small average effects, but individual responders exist, and without blinding the placebo effect swamps everything. People keep stacks running indefinitely out of subscription inertia and spend hundreds to thousands of dollars per year with no feedback loop.
solution: The customer sends the product they already take. A partner packer or compounding pharmacist repackages it and a matched placebo into coded weekly pouches on a randomized ABAB crossover schedule with washout. Outcomes are chosen per compound: sleep and HRV from the customer's own wearable, glucose from an over-the-counter CGM (Stelo or Lingo), and fingerstick or lab draws for ApoB, hs-CRP, ferritin or vitamin D. Pre-registered Bayesian analysis returns 'keep, drop or inconclusive' with the confidence. Offered for supplements only (never prescription drugs), as self-experimentation, not medical advice. An annual 'Stack Audit' rotates one compound every six weeks.
why_now: Over-the-counter CGMs and consumer wearables now supply continuous, cheap outcome data for healthy people; fingerstick lab kits and direct-to-consumer lab ordering are cheap; supplement use is near-universal and skepticism is rising in coverage of 'mostly useless' supplements; and longevity stack culture gives buyers a natural stack to audit.
revenue_model: $129-199 per compound trial plus lab costs at cost; $349 per year Stack Audit; $60 per patient white-label for practitioners; aggregated, consented responder data licensed to academic researchers (never sold to supplement brands, to protect independence).
non_obvious_insight: The most valuable longevity product for the middle class is subtraction. The average effect of most supplements is tiny but individuals differ, and 'proven for me' is the only evidence class people trust. Unlike the industry, this business makes money when people buy less: every dropped supplement saves $20-40 per month, so the service pays for itself in months and the buyer's own spending is the marketing.
first_30_days: Recruit 40 volunteers from biohacking and supplement communities for a $49 pilot on two popular compounds (for example magnesium glycinate for sleep and creatine for energy). Have a local compounding pharmacist or contract packer prepare coded pouches and placebo. Pre-register the analysis in a public spreadsheet, run the trial, and publish an honest 'what we found, including nulls' post. Pitch five functional-medicine practices on white-labeling the kits at $60 per patient.

title: Part-Time Retired Journeymen as Apprentice Supervisors
one_liner: Supervision-as-a-service: retired licensed tradespeople work 2-3 days a week as the supervising journeyman that lets small shops deploy the apprentices and helpers they already have.
customer: 5-25 employee electrical, plumbing and HVAC shops with unlicensed helpers or apprentices, starting in one state with clear ratio and qualifier rules. They pay by the hour.
problem: The headlines say the pipeline is the shortage, but the Gen Z enrollment surge is called a demographic mirage. For many shops the binding constraint is licensed supervision, because ratio rules cap helpers per journeyman. Data-center overtime ($130-170K for journeymen, vendor stat) pulls supervisors off residential work. ABC says most of the 349K 2026 shortfall is retirements, yet retirees hold exactly the scarce credential and are unused.
solution: A vetted, insured bench of retired journeymen and masters placed part-time in shops as supervising journeyman and mentor. The platform verifies licenses, runs employer-of-record or 1099 structure per state rules, handles workers' comp, and automates the apprenticeship hour logs boards require. Shops book blocks such as Tue-Thu 7-3.
why_now: ABC's 2026 gap of 349K is mostly retirement. Data centers now account for nearly a third of the shortage. Immigration enforcement removes helpers, so shops need to hire and supervise local apprentices fast. Trade-school hype is masking a thin pipeline.
revenue_model: Shops pay about $75-110 per hour billed. The platform keeps 20-25% and the retiree keeps the rest. Add $150-250 per month for hour-logging and compliance software.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce good is not labor, it is supervision minutes, and retirees want 16-hour weeks that no normal employer offers. A supervising journeyman unlocks one or two helpers billing at journeyman-adjacent rates, so shops can pay a premium and still gain margin. Rules vary by state and must be verified before launch.
first_30_days: Pick one trade (electrical) in one state with clear ratio rules. Recruit 15 retirees from union retiree groups and lapsing-license lists. Sign 5 shops with 3+ helpers who are idle or under-deployed. Bill the first hours in week 3.

title: A Private IRIS for States and Utilities
one_liner: A consortium of former EPA toxicologists that sells open, peer-reviewed health-risk assessments (nitrate, PFAS mixtures) to state agencies, utilities, insurers and courts.
customer: State environment and health agencies (multi-state membership), large utilities, pollution-liability insurers, state attorneys general, litigation counsel and muni-bond analysts. Agencies and utilities pay membership, and lawyers and insurers pay per project.
problem: Step one: EPA's Office of Research and Development, home of IRIS, was eliminated in 2026, and the nitrate cancer review has stalled since 2023. Step two: EPA cannot update hazard values, while the four PFAS limits proposed for rescission (PFHxS, PFNA, GenX and the Hazard Index) may leave states to decide. Step three: states, utilities, insurers and courts need citable, transparent assessments to set or defend limits, and no one supplies them.
solution: A 'systematic review desk' using pre-registered protocols, external peer review and open publication. First deliverables: a nitrate health assessment and a PFAS mixture assessment, each with a state-adoptable guidance value and a cost-benefit table. Sell expert testimony and state-specific screening levels as add-ons.
why_now: ORD's elimination has released a talent pool of experienced risk assessors at the same moment the PFAS proposals are in comment and the nitrate review is stalled. The 2026 rollback creates a patchwork of state standards.
revenue_model: Consortium membership of $75-250k/yr per state or utility group, $150-500k per assessment, and expert-witness fees.
non_obvious_insight: Government risk-assessment capacity is a public good that is now for sale, and the asset is credibility, not technology. The buyers exist because states, insurers and courts need someone defensible to cite. Independence (open protocols, multi-funder, no client-directed conclusions) is the product.
first_30_days: Recruit three to five ex-ORD or IRIS scientists and incorporate as a public-benefit corporation. Pre-register a nitrate protocol. File an independent analysis in the open EPA PFAS docket to build credibility. Pitch three state agencies and the state drinking-water administrators' association.

title: Vet-Verified Escrow for Puppy Purchases
one_liner: Buyer funds sit in escrow and release to the seller only after a licensed vet exam confirms the animal is healthy and the microchip matches.
customer: First-time online puppy and kitten buyers (mostly Gen Z and millennials), plus ethical breeders, rescues and rehoming sellers who lose sales to scammers. Partner clinics are the fulfillment side and insurers are the third payer.
problem: Pet-purchase scams are a top online-fraud category inside the FTC's record $15.9B of 2025 scam losses. Deposits go by Zelle, Cash App or gift card and are irreversible. Legitimate breeders cannot prove trustworthiness. Sick puppies (parvo and congenital problems) show up days after a sale, and a vet shortage means new-patient slots are scarce, so buyers skip the check.
solution: The buyer pays via card or ACH into escrow. Release requires a 72-hour exam at a partner clinic confirming health, microchip and vaccination records; failure means refund minus fee. Part of the escrow fee pays the clinic for the exam, so the clinic gains a new client with prepaid revenue. The exam visit also enrolls the pet in insurance while it is clean of pre-existing conditions, for an acquisition fee. Extensions: lost-pet reward escrow released on a microchip scan, and stud and rehoming fees.
why_now: Record scam losses and irreversible peer-to-peer payments make buyers and platforms desperate for protection. Only 48.2% of practices proactively recommend insurance, so insurers need better first-year distribution. Clinics are capacity-constrained and want reliable new patients. Delayed-payout marketplace payment APIs make escrow cheap to build.
revenue_model: 4-5% escrow fee, $40-60 insurer acquisition fee per enrolled pet, and clinic exam fees funded from the escrow. Sellers can pay for a verified-breeder badge.
non_obvious_insight: The vet exam is the only trusted, licensed, in-person oracle in the pet-purchase chain, so use it as the escrow release condition. Because the fee funds the visit, the clinic gets a paid new client, which turns the vet shortage into a pull instead of a friction.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 ethical breeders or rescues and 5 clinics in one metro. Build on Stripe Connect delayed payouts. Market to breed groups on Facebook and puppy-advice communities, and offer the first 50 transactions at a discount for testimonials.

title: Battery-Islanded Feeders Instead of Undergrounding
one_liner: Sell utilities islandable rural feeders powered by enrolled home batteries as a cheaper alternative to undergrounding and repeated wildfire power shutoffs.
customer: Wildfire-exposed utilities and co-ops (California, Pacific Northwest, Colorado, Hawaii), funded from wildfire-mitigation capex. Tribal and community microgrids are a secondary buyer.
problem: Undergrounding costs roughly $2-3M or more per mile, and public safety power shutoffs cut power to thousands of homes for days. Home batteries are common (46% storage attach), but each only serves its own house, and utilities cannot use them to keep a whole feeder alive.
solution: A feeder-level controller, smart switch and grid-forming coordination software that lets a segment island when upstream is de-energized, with enrolled home batteries powering critical loads. The same software runs normal VPP dispatch to pay for itself. The utility contracts it as a non-wires wildfire alternative.
why_now: 140k batteries delivered 580 MW on Sept 9, grid-forming inverters are now standard, wildfire budgets are large, and affordability limits undergrounding.
revenue_model: $150-400 per customer-year availability payment from the utility, a controller lease, and VPP revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: The battery is already in the house, and the missing pieces are coordination and a switch. Utilities cannot earn a return on efficiency, but they can on wildfire mitigation capex, and you are competing against $3M per mile.
first_30_days: Approach small co-ops and munis in fire-prone areas. Pick a 200-home feeder with at least 30% battery attach. Propose a paid $40k feasibility study and a pilot using existing devices. Partner with a microgrid-controller vendor.

title: Proof-of-Resident Public Comment
one_liner: Privacy-preserving verification that a public comment or 311 report comes from a real resident, without collecting their identity.
customer: City clerks, county boards, school districts, planning departments and state agencies running public-comment portals.
problem: Governments use GenAI to write documents, and vendors and activists use AI to flood the channels back. Councils and agencies can no longer tell 50 real residents from 5,000 bot-generated comments, so legitimate voices lose weight and hearings are contested.
solution: A comment widget that accepts a zero-knowledge proof from a mobile driver's license or wallet credential, proving residency and unique personhood without revealing name or address. Public dashboards show verified versus unverified counts, and the clerk keeps an audit log.
why_now: Mobile driver's licenses are live in a growing number of states, and wallet-level zero-knowledge proofs shipped in 2025. The signal-to-noise collapse from AI-generated submissions is now visible in procurement and public comment.
revenue_model: $5-30K per year per jurisdiction, with per-verification fees for state agencies and rulemaking dockets. Partner with agenda-management vendors.
non_obvious_insight: Verification without identity is the only approach that a hostile public will accept. Councils do not want a citizen database, they want a trustworthy count.
first_30_days: Build the widget with an open wallet-credential library in a state that supports mobile IDs. Pilot with one city clerk for a controversial hearing. Publish the verified-versus-unverified result.

title: Monetization Compliance-as-Code for Free-to-Play Studios
one_liner: A linter that reads a studio's store and gacha configuration and flags per-country, per-age-band violations, with an auditable rulebook curated by counsel.
customer: Mid-size free-to-play mobile and PC studios and publishers (10-300 staff) selling in the EU, UK, Brazil, Australia and US states.
problem: Rules diverge fast. Brazil's 2025 child-protection law restricts loot boxes for minors (in force in 2026), the EU consumer authorities set 2025 principles on virtual currency pricing, and an EU Digital Fairness Act proposal is expected around late 2026. Roblox age tiers and Discord age checks add age-band segmentation. Studios rely on $400-600 per hour legal memos and hand-checked spreadsheets.
solution: Ingest offer tables, gacha odds, currency bundles and subscription flows from LiveOps exports or APIs. Flag violations per market and age band against a versioned rulebook, produce audit-ready evidence, and gate builds in CI.
why_now: Brazil's restrictions took effect in 2026, the Digital Fairness Act is in the pipeline, and platform age tiers force age-aware storefronts. Enforcement history (Epic's FTC settlements) shows the cost of missing this.
revenue_model: $500-3,000 per month per title, $5-15k onboarding, and a premium tier with counsel-reviewed rule updates.
non_obvious_insight: Games compliance is sold as legal advice, but violations live in JSON: drop tables, prices, labels and flows. That is machine-checkable, law firms sell memos, and nobody ships a linter.
first_30_days: Have a games-regulatory lawyer co-write a 4-market rulebook. Build a linter for one config format (Remote Config plus a gacha CSV). Offer free audits to 10 mobile studios and convert 2 to $1k per month.

title: Plug-In Electrification Kits for Landlords
one_liner: Sell curated no-new-circuit kits (120V heat pump water heaters, window heat pumps, induction, balcony solar) to small landlords and housing authorities as an electrician-light retrofit.
customer: Small landlords (1-50 units), property managers and public housing authorities. Utilities and state HEAR programs co-fund the kits.
problem: Data centers pay electricians 25-30% more, so residential contractors cannot staff jobs. Panel upgrades cost $1,500-5,000. Renters and multifamily have no obvious product, and landlords have no reason to pay for tenants' savings.
solution: A packaged program with approved plug-in devices only (UL 3700 balcony solar in states that legalized it, 120V heat pump water heaters, window heat pumps). Maintenance staff or a handyman installs them. The company handles rebate stacking, a lease addendum and tenant paperwork, an insurance rider, and remote monitoring. It also sells a landlord 'plug-in policy in a box' for HOAs and condo boards.
why_now: Nine states had signed plug-in solar laws by September 2026 and UL 3700 now exists. 120V heat pump water heaters and window heat pumps arrived, and housing-authority window heat pump rollouts show large buyers exist. Labor scarcity makes no-electrician products the path of least resistance.
revenue_model: 15-25% gross margin on $1.5-4k kits, a per-unit administration fee from utility and state programs, and SaaS for portfolio managers.
non_obvious_insight: The electrician shortage is the binding constraint, so design products that do not need one. Renter electrification will run through plug-ins, and whoever writes the landlord's compliance and insurance paperwork controls distribution.
first_30_days: Pick two plug-in-friendly states. Assemble a three-SKU kit from existing vendors. Pitch 20 small landlord associations and two housing authorities. Sell 20 kits. Get an insurer's written OK on the rider language.

title: Vendor-Neutral ELD Log Auditor and DataQs Filer
one_liner: An independent audit that catches the log errors ELD vendors create, and files the FMCSA challenge when they become violations.
customer: Owner-operators and carriers with 1-50 trucks, plus small DOT-compliance consultants who would white-label it. The driver or carrier owner pays.
problem: ELD software errors turn into violations and fines, and vendor support does not fix them. BigRoad reviewers say 'BigRoad could equal BigFines' because it will 'change your duty status randomly on its own'. They also report that it 'automatically switches to driving', that split sleeper 'doesn't work at all', and that a recent update left them unable to sign their logs. A Motive reviewer says 'it tells me I'm two hours into violation yet in the six past days I've driven 41 hours', and another says 'they cannot take off the violations from ELD'. Motive's following-distance alerts also draw complaints: it 'dings you for following too close when cars pass you in the next lane'.
solution: The driver or carrier emails the standard ELD output file, which every FMCSA-registered ELD must be able to produce (49 CFR 395, Appendix A). The system works with any ELD vendor. It rebuilds the duty timeline and flags implausible auto-driving events, unassigned driving, edits without annotations, split-sleeper and personal-conveyance miscalculations, and form-and-manner errors. It sends a weekly 'audit-ready' report before roadside inspections or compliance audits. When a violation is cited, it assembles a DataQs challenge packet (FMCSA's data-correction request) with the log evidence, GPS or fuel-card timestamps and vendor error messages, ready for the carrier to file.
why_now: FMCSA's DataQs site says that as of September 18, 2026 the revised requirements for State data reviews are in effect, with the stated aim that 'drivers receive their proper due process'. That change is 10 days old and makes challenging bad violations a more credible use of a carrier's time. ELD vendors are still shipping regressions (BigRoad reviewers describe updates that broke log signing and split sleeper in 2026), so the error volume keeps producing challenge-worthy events.
revenue_model: $9 per truck per month for the weekly audit. $99-$199 per DataQs packet. A white-label plan for DOT consultants at $500/month for up to 100 trucks. Later: a discount referral to an insurer that rewards clean, audited logs.
non_obvious_insight: Drivers cannot tell whether the ELD or the driver is wrong, and the vendor has no incentive to tell them. The federal ELD standard gives an open data pipe, so a third party can check any vendor's logs without a vendor integration, and the answer is more credible because the auditor does not sell ELDs. Evidence: BigRoad ELD app reviews (duty status flips, split sleeper broken, 'BigFines') at https://itunes.apple.com/us/rss/customerreviews/id=674704833/sortby=mostrecent/xml. Motive reviews (false violation time, violations the vendor cannot remove, following-distance algorithm complaints) at https://www.trustpilot.com/review/gomotive.com. The DataQs process and the Sept 18, 2026 change are on FMCSA's own page at https://dataqs.fmcsa.dot.gov/. Carriers already pay for DataQs help, so the willingness to pay is proven. The new part is vendor-neutral log analysis with a challenge packet ready to file.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: read the ELD output file spec, build a parser using FMCSA's sample files and one test ELD, and write the 8 error checks. Days 10-20: recruit 10 owner-operators from trucker Facebook groups and forums for a free audit of their last 8 days. Days 20-30: show each one the specific errors found, charge for the first DataQs packets, and sign 2-3 DOT consultants for the white-label plan. Get a compliance professional to review the packet format.

title: Market Surveillance for Entertainment Prediction Markets
one_liner: Sportradar-style integrity monitoring for the boom in prediction-market contracts on awards, charts, box office and game releases, where insiders and bot farms can swing outcomes.
customer: CFTC-regulated prediction-market exchanges and brokers that list entertainment contracts (Kalshi-type venues and the betting and brokerage firms entering the space). Secondary buyers are rights holders and award bodies (studios, labels, game publishers, guilds) that want to know when their confidential information is being traded.
problem: Per the briefing, Kalshi went from about $11B to $22B valuation in 2026, entertainment and awards are already about 11% of its activity, and states are fighting the venues. Exchanges must list contracts that are not readily susceptible to manipulation and run surveillance, but their tooling is built for sports and finance. Entertainment outcomes can be moved by insiders (PR staff, awards accountants, streaming-platform employees, contractors who know game release dates), by bot-farmed streams and votes, by review-bombing, and by leaked builds and schedules. Resolution sources (Spotify charts, Rotten Tomatoes, Steam counts, box office) are each gameable in a different way.
solution: (1) A 'contract risk review' done before an entertainment market lists: score the resolution source for manipulability (cost to swing it, for example streams or votes needed) and the insider population (who knows the outcome and how many people), then recommend rules such as delayed settlement, position limits and source hierarchies. (2) Live surveillance that flags anomalous trading, such as fresh accounts trading ahead of announcements or positions timed with leak or stream-spike signals, cross-referenced with external manipulation indicators (streaming bot networks, vote farms). (3) Investigation and referral packages for exchanges and regulators. (4) A rights-holder subscription that alerts when a contract references their confidential events.
why_now: Kalshi's valuation doubled in five months and new entrants are listing culture contracts. Multiple states are attacking event contracts, so demonstrable surveillance is now a legal-defense asset. GTA VI launches 19 Nov 2026 and Q4 award season and Spotify Wrapped create dense culture-contract activity. AI-cheap bot streaming and vote farms lower manipulation costs, and Chainalysis notes scam tooling now sells for about $50 (per briefing).
revenue_model: Annual retainer of $60-250k per exchange for the surveillance feed. $2-10k per contract risk review. Rights-holder alert subscriptions of $2-5k/month. Hourly investigation and expert-witness work.
non_obvious_insight: Sports-integrity firms never learned how an awards accountant or a streaming intern leaks, and entertainment insiders are far more numerous and less regulated than athletes. Resolution sources are commercial dashboards, not referees. The buyer's budget is really a legal-defense budget for defending the product state by state.
first_30_days: One fraud/market-abuse analyst plus one music/film/game data specialist. Publish a 'manipulation cost' analysis of the 10 most-traded entertainment contracts (Oscar categories, Spotify top artist, Steam concurrent players, Rotten Tomatoes scores) and send it to compliance heads at 5 exchanges. Offer a 30-day paid pilot review of upcoming contracts (GTA VI launch, award season) at $10-15k.

title: Provider-in-Residence: Vacant Units Become Childcare
one_liner: Convert vacant ground-floor apartments in lease-up buildings into licensed family child care homes run by vetted early-educator residents, paid for out of the landlord's existing concession budget.
customer: Multifamily owners and operators in concession-heavy Sun Belt markets (success fee per activated unit), family child care entrepreneurs (a back-office subscription), and residents or subsidy programs paying tuition.
problem: Licensed capacity is barely growing (centers +1.5% and family homes +4.3% in 2024) while two children in center care cost more than rent in every state and the average childcare worker earns about $33,000. Meanwhile 1.2M apartment units are in lease-up, concessions run 15.8% of stabilized units (37% in Austin), it takes 34 days to lease, and owners are giving away free months on units that could earn nothing better.
solution: Pre-screen buildings for ground-floor 2-3 bedroom units that pass local family child care home rules (which in many states are treated as residential use). Recruit early educators, nannies and ex-teachers, fit out the unit (child-proofing, egress), coach them through licensing, and lease them the unit at a discount in place of the concession, so they live and work there. Resident families get priority. The operator handles enrollment, billing, subsidy paperwork, insurance and a shared substitute pool across buildings.
why_now: The lease-up glut has made concessions a real, measurable budget line and landlords are experimenting with anything that fills units or improves retention. The 2025-26 tax changes (DCFSA raised to $7,500, larger 45F credit) push employers and families toward childcare spending. Family child care homes are the fastest-growing licensed segment.
revenue_model: Landlord success fee of about $2-4K per activated unit (about one to two months of rent), 6-8% of tuition for back-office and subsidy handling, and a group insurance margin.
non_obvious_insight: A childcare seat is worth about $1,300 a month to a family, far more than a month of free rent is to a prospect, and a family with a child in the building is far less likely to move. The concession budget is already spent, and spending it on seats produces supply in a category where zoning is usually on your side.
first_30_days: Pick one metro with high concessions such as Austin, Phoenix, Atlanta or Nashville and check the state's family-home rules (ratios, floor level, egress). Pitch 5 lease-up operators and sign two letters of intent for 2-3 units each. Recruit three providers through early-educator communities and begin licensing, aiming for first enrollments by month four or five.

title: Fire-Season Vaults for Fandom Collectors
one_liner: Red-Flag-Warning-triggered pickup and insured off-site storage for graded cards, comics, sealed games and memorabilia kept in wildfire-zone homes.
customer: Collectors holding $50K-$2M of graded trading cards, comics, sealed games and signed memorabilia in wildfire-zone ZIPs or on last-resort plans such as the California FAIR Plan (696,562 policies in June 2026).
problem: A closet of graded cards can be worth more than the contents limit on a distressed-market homeowners policy. Collectibles are usually capped or need scheduling, which retreating carriers avoid. Evacuations give minutes. Vaults exist, but storage is a one-time decision with no urgency trigger, and nobody sells 'fire season' as a product.
solution: Three steps. (1) Photograph and catalog the collection with a card-scanning app and a live price feed, producing a claim-ready inventory. (2) From June to November, the top slice of value moves to a bonded vault under agreed-value cover from a specialty coverholder. (3) The remainder goes in a pre-tagged go-case, and on a Red Flag Warning or evacuation warning within N miles a bonded courier collects it within 4 hours, or the owner drops it at a partner card shop. Everything is returned in December.
why_now: The trading-card boom (Pokemon at 85B+ cards, a $28M Kickstarter TCG, blind-box resale above RMB 1,000 with VCs funding the resale layer) has turned closets into six-figure assets. FAIR Plan exposure hit $768B (secondary source) with a 29.1% rate hike. New carriers expanding under California's Sustainable Insurance Strategy have said nothing about scheduled personal property.
revenue_model: Annual fee of about 0.6-1.2% of stored declared value (storage plus insurance), a $150-400 courier trigger fee per activation, and commission on the agreed-value policy. An average $250K customer is worth about $2.5K a year.
non_obvious_insight: Insurers are retreating from the house, not from the objects. Fandom wealth is small, portable and already authenticated (slab cert numbers), so it is the one wildfire-zone asset you can move in a single trip and value without an adjuster. The business is logistics plus underwriting data, not a vault.
first_30_days: Pre-sell 30 founding memberships through Discord, Reddit and 10 card and comic shops in fire-prone ZIPs (Altadena, Topanga, Santa Rosa, Boulder foothills). Partner with an existing vault and a Lloyd's coverholder rather than building either. Run the first live drill when Santa Ana wind season starts in October-November.

title: Human Failover Retainer for Agent-Run Businesses
one_liner: Backup-generator economics for know-how: a retained, drilled bench of human operators that takes over within hours when a company's AI agents fail.
customer: Owners and COOs of 10-200 person companies that replaced back-office headcount with AI agents. First niche: freight brokerages (dispatch, carrier onboarding, load booking). Then medical billing firms, property managers, insurance agencies and 3PLs.
problem: After automation, the people who knew the manual process leave. Then a model deprecation, provider outage, prompt regression, API key ban or payment-processor freeze halts revenue, and nobody remembers how to do the job by hand. Cloud disaster-recovery plans protect servers, not the tacit process knowledge. That skill decays every month the automation succeeds.
solution: A $1.5-6k/month retainer. Phase 1: shadow the process while it still lives in staff heads and write executable runbooks and checklists. Phase 2: keep a pre-vetted bench of remote operators (ex-dispatchers, ex-billers) who sample live work weekly, so they stay current. Phase 3: run quarterly 'lights-out drills' that switch the agents off for four hours and measure time to recover. Guarantee takeover within two hours, billed hourly on activation. The bench's weekly sampling doubles as gold-label QA that flags agent drift, so the retainer also improves the agents.
why_now: 2025-26 brought large cloud and LLM-API outages (for example the October 2025 AWS us-east-1 incident), fast model deprecation cycles, and boards booking headcount cuts on the strength of agents. Insurers are starting to ask about AI-related business-interruption exposure, which gives a compliance reason to buy.
revenue_model: Monthly retainer tiered by process criticality; activation fees at $60-120 per operator-hour; drill and runbook-documentation fees; an insurer or broker referral channel that offers premium credits for a documented failover plan.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody buys a generator until the blackout, but unlike a generator the failover gets more expensive the more successful the AI rollout is, because human know-how atrophies. The best time to sell is right after a company celebrates automation savings, and the CFO can fund the retainer out of those savings. It is a services business that looks like insurance, with recurring revenue, and a bench of a few dozen part-timers can cover many clients.
first_30_days: Pick freight brokerage and find 40 brokers advertising AI dispatch or quoting. Offer a free two-hour 'lights-out drill' to about 10 of them: switch off the agents, time the recovery and hand back a one-page automation-debt score. Recruit 6 part-time ex-dispatchers as the bench. Convert 3 drill participants to $1.5-2.5k/month retainers. Package the outputs as a case study.

title: Lot Vault: Reagent Warranty Claims and Lot Registry
one_liner: A photo-the-label app that files unclaimed reagent-guarantee refunds for labs, quietly builds the only lot-level reagent performance database, and then group-buys locked good lots for small labs.
customer: Lab managers and PIs in organoid, iPSC, primary-immune-cell and antibody-heavy labs (about $79-199/month per lab). Core facilities and departments with central purchasing pay for the site-wide tier. Later, challenger reagent vendors and distributors pay for lot-level analytics.
problem: Every experienced postdoc knows the hidden variable behind failed experiments is the reagent lot: FBS, Matrigel/BME, B27, human serum, antibodies, polymerases. A lot that passes the vendor's certificate of analysis can still kill your organoids, and nobody logs lot numbers. Vendors' satisfaction guarantees require the lot number, images and a claim inside a time window, so postdocs almost never file. Money goes unclaimed. Six labs across town hit the same bad lot and never find out. When a good lot runs out, a two-year experimental series has to be re-validated.
solution: Wedge: a phone app where the postdoc snaps the vial label and taps 'worked' or 'failed', with optional gel or blot photos. On 'failed' it drafts the vendor guarantee claim with lot, dates and images, and tracks the credit. On 'worked' it logs the lot against the user's cell type and assay. Over time this becomes a crowd-sourced registry: 'Matrigel lot X: 7 of 9 organoid labs report failure.' Phase 2: when a lot shows good in at least 5 labs, the company negotiates a vendor lot reservation and runs a pooled group buy. Small labs get a locked lot for 12-24 months without needing 100 bottles of freezer space. The company takes a 10-15% margin.
why_now: NIH funding disruption and higher reagent prices from tariffs (verify current tariff levels) make labs care about every wasted dollar in 2025-26. Vision LLMs make label OCR and claim drafting almost free. Reproducibility pressure is high and the NIH is pushing rigor. Vendors are consolidating, and challenger brands need a credible independent signal to displace incumbents.
revenue_model: Subscription per lab or per core. A 10-15% margin on group-buy locked-lot sales. Success-fee or flat fee on recovered credits. Later, paid lot-analytics dashboards for challenger vendors and distributors.
non_obvious_insight: The certificate of analysis tests the vendor's assay, not yours. The only real lot-quality signal is 'the lab down the hall using my cell type', and that signal already circulates informally by hallway lore. Nobody has digitized it because no single lab has enough data. The warranty-claim refund is the Trojan horse: it gives the user immediate ROI, so people log lot numbers without being asked, and it produces the data moat.
first_30_days: Build a no-code MVP: a forwarding inbox plus a form that pulls lot number and catalog number and drafts claim emails. Recruit 15 labs from organoid and iPSC Slack and Discord channels and postdoc association lists. Offer 3 months free plus a 'we file it for you' concierge. File the first 30 claims by hand to learn each vendor's rules. Show each lab the dollars recovered. Convert to $99/month once the first credit lands. In parallel, pick one product (for example BME or FBS) and quote a pooled lot reservation to 10 pilot labs.

title: Bonded Claims: Bug Bounties for Product Labels
one_liner: Brands post a forfeitable bond behind a testable label claim, and anyone can buy the product, get it lab-tested and collect the bond if the claim is false.
customer: Mid-size DTC supplement, protein, baby-food and pet-food brands whose 'third-party tested' or 'heavy-metal free' claims are doubted, plus retail and marketplace buyers who want evidence and insurers.
problem: Label claims cannot be checked on the shelf. Certifications are one-time and paid for by the certified. Heavy-metal and potency class actions are routine, and gray-market peptide vendors forge certificates of analysis (FDA warning letters to seven online sellers, Mar 2026). Honest brands cannot distinguish themselves.
solution: A claim registry. The brand states a specific, machine-checkable claim (for example lead below X per serving, or label potency within 10%), posts a $10-50k bond in escrow and accepts a protocol: retail-purchased units, an accredited lab, and blinded replicates. Challengers pay for tests or use subsidised credits, and a neutral panel confirms chain of custody. A failed claim pays the challenger and forfeits the bond and badge. A claim that survives N challenges earns a 'survived challenge' tier that retail buyers can query by API.
why_now: Finnrick has now published 10,000+ independent peptide tests, proving that crowds will fund lab tests of vendors. Heavy-metal exposés and lawsuits keep recurring. Stablecoin and card-hold escrow make small bonds cheap to run. Retailers want a liability shield for clean-label shelves.
revenue_model: $2-5k annual listing fee, a 1-3% bond-management fee, challenge-processing fees, and retailer API licences.
non_obvious_insight: Bug bounties worked in software because they turn hostile sceptics into paid auditors. Physical-goods certification does the opposite and pays friendly auditors. A bond makes the brand fund the scepticism, and only honest brands can afford to post one, which gives the badge a real price premium.
first_30_days: Approach 10 clean-label brands that already publish certificates of analysis (creatine, collagen, omega-3, kids' vitamins) and pitch it as cheaper than class-action defence. Sign one ISO 17025 lab for a fixed test panel. Run a public 'challenge week' with a supplement community, using a standard escrow account.

title: Surety Bonds for Agent Operators
one_liner: A customs bond for bots: agent operators post a surety-backed bond so sites, APIs and merchants can say yes to their agents and get paid if the agents misbehave.
customer: Mid-size vendors of browser, shopping and procurement agents ($1M-$50M ARR) whose agents get blocked or throttled. They pay for the bond and credential. Merchants and API providers consume the signal for free.
problem: Agent identity schemes (signed agents, know-your-agent) say who an agent is, not who pays when it scrapes abusively, mis-buys or triggers chargebacks. Agents are cheap to recreate, so identity carries no cost of failure. Bots are now 57.4% of requests, so sites default to blocking. After the August 2026 Ninth Circuit Comet ruling, blocking has to rest on contract and technical measures, so sites need a concrete reason to let agents in.
solution: Underwrite the operator (KYB, behavior review, volume caps). Issue a surety or insurer-backed bond ($25k-$1M penal sum) plus a signed credential that plugs into existing agent-auth headers and protocols. Sites whitelist a bonded lane with higher rate limits. A small claims desk pays on signed request logs. Wedge: agent vendors selling into mid-market merchants and B2B API providers that would create a bonded lane in their bot rules.
why_now: Bots overtook humans in 2026, and the Ninth Circuit ruling shifts blocking to contract terms. Neither Visa nor Mastercard has a binding agent-dispute rule, and Visa's merchant dispute threshold tightened to 1.5% in April 2026, so merchants are risk-averse. Bonding has been proposed only in academic papers so far, and no product exists.
revenue_model: Bond premium share (typically 1-3% of penal sum per year) plus a $500-$5,000/month underwriting and credential fee, plus surety agency commission.
non_obvious_insight: Trust that scales in commerce rests on bonds, not identity. Freight brokers, contractors and customs brokers all post bonds. A bond makes an operator's reputation costly to abandon, and a site only has to trust the surety, not the operator.
first_30_days: Partner with a small surety agency or MGA to draft a miscellaneous bond form and a claims evidence standard. Recruit 5 agent vendors that merchants block and 5 merchants or API providers willing to whitelist. Sell the first 3 pilot bonds at $500-$1,500 per year plus a setup fee.

title: Help-Desk Reset Firewall for MSPs
one_liner: A plug-in for ConnectWise, Autotask and HaloPSA that makes it impossible for a technician to reset a password or MFA without out-of-band verification and manager approval.
customer: MSPs and outsourced IT help desks serving SMBs, priced per technician.
problem: IT help desks are a named target of voice deepfakes, and one report says over half of CISOs have seen a successful attack. An MSP technician is a single point of compromise for dozens of client tenants, and techs judge identity by voice and by facts attackers already have. SMB clients have no security team to catch it.
solution: A reset gate inside the ticket. MFA resets, password resets and new-device enrollments require verification through a contact and number pulled from the client's HR system or PSA (never from the caller), a manager approval push, a cooling-off delay with notification to the user's existing devices, and risk scoring (new country, odd hours). Evidence is stored for insurer questionnaires.
why_now: Help-desk social engineering drove major 2025 intrusions, voice cloning removes the tell, and insurers now ask about caller verification. Enterprise help-desk verification vendors ignore the MSP channel.
revenue_model: $15-30 per technician per month plus $1 per client user per month.
non_obvious_insight: MSPs are the most leveraged and least-served target. The control is a process lock, not a detector, so it does not decay when deepfakes improve, and insurance-renewal pressure makes it a required purchase.
first_30_days: Build it as a ConnectWise Manage/HaloPSA webhook plus a Teams approval bot. Recruit 10 MSPs from MSP peer groups and forums at $299 per month, and show the insurance-renewal benefit.
